title: Sunlight: make a safer plan
subtitle: Spring 2 • Week 2 • Evidence, labels and everyday choices
objective: Explain why sunlight can harm eyes and choose sensible ways to reduce exposure.

sow.exactOutcome: Explain that the Sun's light can be dangerous and how to protect our eyes (links PSHE).
sow.alignment: Direct match to the named outcome. The lesson is a 40-minute exemplar, with optional greater depth; no accreditation completion is claimed.

priorLearning: Everyday objects can be described by what we observe.
Use a labelled diagram or evidence card to explain a choice.
success: Explain that sunlight can damage eyes.
Choose suitable UV-filtering sunglasses, a brimmed hat and shade.
Keep the rule: never look directly at the Sun.

vocabulary.meaning: Radiation in sunlight that we cannot see and that can harm eyes and skin.
Something that reduces exposure or harm.
To send radiation back from a surface.

equipment: Printed scenario and equipment cards; optional empty sunglasses packaging with clear UV information; paper and pens.
preparation: Use the supplied fictional cards, not pupils’ personal eyewear, for judgments.
Read the linked NHS/RNIB guidance. Follow the school’s normal outdoor arrangements and individual pupil plans.
safety: This is an indoor planning lesson: never look directly at the Sun or stare into bright reflections.
Never test protection by looking at the Sun through lenses, plastic, a camera, binoculars or a telescope.
Do not use UV lamps or test products on pupils. Sunglasses are for ordinary outdoor protection, not Sun viewing.
practicalAlternative: The full lesson is a paper-based decision task. No outdoor exposure, equipment testing or online video is required.

misconceptions.correction: Darkness shows reduced visible light; it does not by itself confirm UV protection.
misconceptions.check: Ask which card provides UV evidence.

misconceptions.claim: Sunglasses make looking directly at the Sun safe.
misconceptions.correction: Ordinary sunglasses do not make direct Sun viewing safe.
misconceptions.check: Ask for the rule that always remains.

misconceptions.correction: Reflected sunlight can also reach us; combine suitable protection.

access.supported: Choose one route: short choices, word bank and pointing or adult-scribed explanation; keep the same science goal.
access.standard: Use the evidence provided to record a decision and explain the science in short sentences.
access.stretch: Apply the same core idea to a changed setup, identify a limitation and justify a better decision.
access.regulation: Preview the sequence and equipment. Offer seated observation, a quiet paper route, partner rehearsal and a pass. Never require public performance or a darkened room.

slides.title: Plan an outdoor break
body: No one looks at the Sun.
slides.notes: State clearly that this is an indoor planning activity. The lesson is about sensible choices, not testing limits of exposure.

slides.title: Three light clues
body: 1. Does the Sun give out light?
3. Is staring at the Sun a safe test?
slides.notes: Answers yes, yes, no. Correct the third immediately; no pupil should demonstrate or rehearse unsafe Sun viewing.

slides.title: Some sunlight is invisible
body: UV is invisible to our eyes.
slides.notes: Think aloud: “I cannot judge UV by how bright or hot I feel. This diagram separates two kinds of radiation; the boxes do not show their amounts. I choose protection before exposure.” Do not imply UV is the only mechanism of harm from direct Sun viewing.

visual.title: Sunlight includes more than we can see
visual.description: The diagram separates visible light and invisible ultraviolet in sunlight. The bands are categories, not proportions or a complete spectrum.

elements.text:
Visible light
Our eyes detect it.
Schematic categories: not amounts or a full spectrum.

slides.title: I read the protection evidence
body: I also plan shade and a hat.
slides.notes: Think aloud: “A dark-looking lens changes visible light. I need reliable information about UV filtering and suitable fit. In real life an adult checks the product through a reputable supplier or optician.” Ordinary sunglasses never make staring at the Sun safe.

visual.title: UV protection is a property of the lens
visual.description: Incoming UV is strongly reduced by a suitable UV-filtering lens. Some visible light passes through. The schematic is not a measured transmission graph.

elements.text: Lens darkness alone cannot confirm UV protection.

slides.title: Reflection matters as well
slides.notes: Shares I do time. Think aloud: “Facing away is not a complete protection plan. Light can arrive from another direction. I still use suitable sunglasses, a hat and shade.” This is a path model, not a measured dose estimate.

visual.title: Sunlight can arrive from another direction
visual.description: A schematic ray from the Sun reflects from water towards a person. This illustrates why reflected sunlight also matters for protection, without an instruction to look into the Sun or reflection.

elements.text: Never look at the Sun or stare into its bright reflection.

slides.title: Choose the strongest kit
slides.notes: Pairs receive kit cards A–D. A has only a dark tint claim; B is a constructed verified suitable UV-filtering option. Select B and add C/D. Do not teach pupils to trust any unverified sticker in the real world.

rows: Dark lenses; UV protection not confirmed
Reliable check confirms suitable UV protection and fit
table.caption: Constructed teaching evidence

slides.prompt: W1. Which plan is supported by the evidence?
slides.reveal: Choose B with a hat and shade. A’s darkness alone is not enough.

slides.title: Repair the risky message
body: Message: “Wear sunglasses, then watch the Sun.”
Keep protection and the no-looking rule.
slides.notes: Ask every pair to reject the message and provide a replacement. Give a quiet written route. Then introduce scenario E by water and F with only dark unverified glasses: neither licenses direct viewing or guessing protection.
slides.prompt: W2. What must our message always say?
slides.reveal: Never look directly at the Sun. Suitable sunglasses reduce ordinary exposure; they do not make Sun viewing safe.

slides.title: Which is the safest science claim?
slides.notes: If pupils choose A, distinguish visible tint from UV filtering. If B, restate the direct-viewing prohibition before moving on.

options.text: Very dark lenses prove good UV protection.
options.feedback: Tint alone does not confirm UV filtering; reliable product information is needed.

options.text: Sunglasses let us stare at the Sun safely.
options.feedback: Ordinary sunglasses do not make direct Sun viewing safe.

options.text: Use suitable UV protection, a hat and shade; never look directly at the Sun.
options.feedback: This combines sensible protection and preserves the essential no-looking rule.

slides.title: Choose your investigation route
body: Make a decision with missing evidence.
slides.notes: Give one route only, selected with the pupil. The shared evidence page supports every route. The independent task is a decision brief, not a real exposure trial. An adult can scribe the pupil’s reasons. Use the supplied verified fictional product information; never judge a real pupil’s glasses by colour alone.

slides.title: Use the evidence
body: Read or point to one clue.
slides.notes: Shares the 12-minute independent stage. The independent task is a decision brief, not a real exposure trial. An adult can scribe the pupil’s reasons. Use the supplied verified fictional product information; never judge a real pupil’s glasses by colour alone.

slides.title: Make your own science record
body: Use a diagram, words or speech.
Check one answer with the evidence.
slides.notes: Allow ten minutes of independent response after the two-minute setup. The independent task is a decision brief, not a real exposure trial. An adult can scribe the pupil’s reasons. Use the supplied verified fictional product information; never judge a real pupil’s glasses by colour alone.

slides.title: Check and improve
body: Does my answer match the evidence?
slides.notes: Shares the independent stage. Ask the pupil to point to the clue supporting their answer; accept a spoken correction or changed choice.

slides.title: Lundy loop: improve our account
body: Choose how to share one idea.
Use evidence to improve our account.
slides.notes: Give a private or paired option. Adopt one scientifically sound pupil revision in the class explanation and name the change. No public ranking.
slides.prompt: Which sentence must stay in every plan?
slides.reveal: Never look directly at the Sun, even when wearing ordinary sunglasses.

slides.title: Three quick checks
body: E1. Why do we protect our eyes from sunlight?
E2. Name two ways to reduce exposure.
E3. Do ordinary sunglasses make Sun viewing safe?
slides.notes: Collect brief individual answers. Secure core requires the main idea and a relevant reason. Revisit the relevant worked diagram next lesson if the explanation reverses cause and effect.
slides.reveal: See the teacher answer guide for the three checks.

pupilPages.title: Evidence: kit and scenario cards
pupilPages.intro: Constructed planning cases. Do not test any item by looking at the Sun.

cards.title: A • Dark lenses
cards.text: The glasses are dark. Their UV protection has not been confirmed.

cards.title: B • Checked glasses
cards.text: A reliable check confirms suitable UV protection and a good fit for the wearer.

cards.title: C • Brimmed hat
cards.text: A wide brim provides extra shade around the face and eyes.

cards.title: D • Shaded area
cards.text: A suitable shaded place is available for the break.

cards.title: E • Beside water
cards.text: Bright sunlight can reflect from the water. The group is planning an outdoor break.

cards.title: F • Missing protection
cards.text: Only unverified dark glasses are available. A supervised indoor option is available.

blocks.prompt: W1. Choose a kit from A–D. Explain one choice.
W2. Correct: “Sunglasses make Sun watching safe.”

pupilPages.title: Route 1 • Choose and explain
pupilPages.intro: Word bank: UV / shade / hat / never.

blocks.prompt: S1. Which glasses have useful protection evidence?
S2. Choose two extra ways to reduce exposure from cards C and D.
S3. Can we see UV with our eyes?
S4. Complete the rule: __ look directly at the Sun.
S5. Why is lens darkness alone not enough information?

pupilPages.title: Route 2 • Write a useful safety brief
pupilPages.intro: Use scenario E beside water. Write for another pupil.

blocks.prompt: T1. Explain two ways sunlight could reach the group.
T2. Choose glasses A or B and explain the evidence.
T3. Add two practical parts to the protection plan.
T4. Write the rule about looking at the Sun.
T5. Explain why the plan reduces exposure but does not make every action safe.

pupilPages.title: Route 3 • Make a decision under uncertainty
pupilPages.intro: Use scenario F. Do not guess that dark glasses have UV protection.

blocks.prompt: X1. What information is missing?
X2. Choose a sensible immediate plan using the available options.
X3. How could an adult check suitable eyewear for a future outdoor break?
X4. Explain why “it does not feel bright” is not a reliable UV test.

pupilPages.title: Exit and reflection
pupilPages.intro: Point, draw, write or tell an adult.

blocks.prompt: E1. Why do we protect our eyes from sunlight?
E2. Name two ways to reduce exposure.
E3. Do ordinary sunglasses make Sun viewing safe?
R1. Which idea did you improve after hearing evidence?
R2. What would you investigate or ask next?

answers.label: Retrieval 1–3
answers.answer: 1 yes. 2 yes. 3 no; never look directly at the Sun.

answers.label: We do W1–W2
answers.answer: W1 B has the relevant UV and fit evidence; add C and D. A is unconfirmed. W2 never look directly at the Sun. Suitable sunglasses are for ordinary exposure, not staring at it.

answers.label: Hinge
answers.answer: Third option correct. Dark tint does not itself confirm UV protection, and ordinary sunglasses do not permit Sun viewing.

answers.label: S1–S5
answers.answer: S1 B. S2 wide-brimmed hat and shade. S3 no. S4 never. S5 darkness describes visible light transmission, not confirmed UV filtering.

answers.label: T1–T5
answers.answer: T1 direct sunlight and reflected sunlight from water. T2 B because reliable evidence confirms suitable UV protection and fit. T3 hat and shade. T4 never look directly at the Sun. T5 exposure is reduced, but ordinary sunglasses do not make direct viewing safe and protection is not an unlimited guarantee.

answers.label: X1–X4
answers.answer: X1 reliable UV protection and suitable fit information. X2 use the supervised indoor option and ask an adult to plan suitable protection before going out; do not improvise a Sun test. X3 check reputable product information or consult an optician; an adult should also check fit. X4 UV is invisible, so perceived brightness alone is insufficient.

answers.label: Exit E1–E3
answers.answer: E1 sunlight can harm eyes. E2 any two: suitable UV-filtering sunglasses, wide-brimmed hat, shade. E3 no.

answers.label: R1–R2
answers.answer: Responses vary. Credit a science-related revision or relevant next question. A pass or private response is acceptable; preferences have no fixed right answer.

teacherNotes: 40 minutes: opening 2; retrieval 3; I do 7; We do 8; hinge 3; You do 12; review 3; exit 2. Zero-minute slides share the stage time.
BUILD follows the user’s Year 3 science anchor with age-respectful materials for secondary pupils. Routes are adjustable access choices, not fixed groups or diagnoses.
Every core task can run from the printed evidence. Do not present constructed teaching evidence as observations pupils made. A pupil’s spoken reasoning carries the same scientific value as writing.
Keep advice proportionate and practical. No frightening images or personal medical stories are required. The lesson teaches ordinary prevention, not diagnosis or a product certification test.

The NHS and RNIB guidance provides the public-health basis. The diagrams simplify categories and pathways; they do not quantify an individual pupil’s exposure or show a complete electromagnetic spectrum.

HTML We do: pupils choose a prediction, test it against the user-controlled SVG model or supplied evidence, then explain or revise. The shared paper cases and W1/W2 prompts provide the equivalent classroom discussion without a device. Any animation is a teaching model, not filmed experimental evidence.
